newsitem.title: USA: Clinton invites Arafat, Netanyahu for talks.
newsitem.headline: Clinton invites Arafat, Netanyahu for talks.

text.p: President Bill Clinton said on Sunday that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat would visit Washington this week to try to end the recent Middle East violence.

Clinton said in a brief news conference that Arafat and Netanyahu had accepted his invitation to Washington, but a Palestinian official said that Arafat had withheld his assent, insisting on the presence of Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak.

Speaking in the White House Rose Garden, Clinton said that Mubarak and Jordan's King Hussein had also been invited to the meetings, which White House officials said were tentatively scheduled to take place on Tuesday and Wednesday.

With just over five weeks to go until the Nov. 5, election, the summit quickly took on political overtones, with the two top Republicans in Congress warning Clinton against pressuring Israel to adopt any unilateral concessions.
Israel's ambassador to the United States, Eliahu Ben-Elissar, predicted the summit would be a success, as both knew the stakes for Clinton were high.
"I believe this summit is not going to fail, and if you ask me how I can be that confident, nobody is going to dare to do this to President Clinton," he told CNN from New York.
Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa told CBS television that Mubarak wanted some assurance that Israel would honour its past agreements with the Palestinians before agreeing to come.
A Palestinian official told Reuters in Gaza that Clinton had telephoned Arafat to invite him to Washington, adding: "Arafat insisted on the participation of ... Mubarak."
"Clinton and Arafat agreed to continue contacts with Mubarak to convince him to attend," the Palestinian official added, saying Arafat would fly to Cairo on Monday.

A White House spokesman confirmed that Clinton had spoken to Arafat, Netanyahu, Hussein of Jordan and Mubarak on Sunday afternoon, adding the United States "fully expects" Arafat to come to Washington, regardless of Mubarak's presence.

Clinton called for the summit to help end five days of clashes in which 55 Palestinians and 14 Israelis have died following Israel's opening of an archaeological tunnel near Jerusalem's al-Aqsa mosque, Islam's third-holiest site.

"The loss of life and the tragedy of the violence in the Middle East this week have been a terrible development for the Israeli and the Palestinian people, a blow to all those who have worked for a lasting peace, an encouragement to those who oppose a lasting peace," Clinton said.

"I am prepared to do everything in my power to help the Israelis and the Palestinians end the violence and begin the peace process again," he said. "We have to return to the path of peace along which they have already travelled so far."
Netanyahu told ABC Television he was eager for the talks and would respect existing agreements, but declined to say whether he might close the tunnel to help calm the situation.
"I'm committed to the peace agreements. I hope that Arafat is committed as well," he said. "He has to keep his side of the bargain ... to keep law and order and to fight terrorism."
Asked why Netanyahu and Arafat were willing to come to Washington, Clinton replied:
"I think that they're both concerned about the way that events have spun out of control, about the loss of life, the injury, the eruption of old tensions and bitterness," he said.
"And I believe they want to try to get beyond that and go back to moving toward the path of peace. I don't think they would be coming here if they didn't," Clinton added.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters the tentative plan was for the leaders to hold bilateral meetings on Tuesday, possibly followed by a wider meeting. He said there would probably be further talks on Wednesday.

Republican challenger Bob Dole issued a brief statement on Sunday saying he hoped the meeting would be a step toward ending the violence there. While he did not mention Clinton by name, Dole said the latest outbreak of violence was "a painful reminder that too many differences have been glossed over in earlier stages of the peace process."
Dole, campaigning in Bal Harbour, Florida, also warned that the United States could not impose a solution and should act only as "friend and facilitator."
